operations.note: Kobe Airport removed -- the ocean reclaims the island, not just its buildings. returnToSea unions the demolish area directly into World.sea, so it renders as open water with a fresh coastline stroke and is permanently exempt from ever counting as land content again (see ops/demolish.py). An earlier draft used leaveLanduse=brownfield instead -- that models 'buildings cleared, ground stays dry land', the wrong operation for 'let the sea take it back'; kept as a separate opt-in for demolishes where the ground genuinely stays land. Demolish polygon is the real (concave) union of every aeroway=*, landuse/leisure area, and building within 3500m of the field -- reusing parse.land_content()'s own definition of 'land', the same test sea.py trusts for carving the coastline -- restricted to the connected component nearest the airport point, buffered 50m and simplified to 32 vertices. Not a hand-guessed circle, and deliberately NOT that union's convex hull: hulling it bridged the water gap toward Port Island and would have swept up real residential buildings there. Verified clean (0 features intersect the final polygon's 2m-shrunk interior) and verified NOT over-reaching (every named building actually caught is airport infrastructure or the small staff-housing block that turns out to sit on the island itself, confirmed by coordinates falling inside the aeroway-only bounding envelope). Tests the graph-cascade pruning (ops/demolish.py) against real topology: the island's own road network plus the connecting bridge from Port Island must all be eaten back to the first real junction, never left as a stub.

Directorate forward hangar sited in the mountain valley northwest of downtown, well past the last mapped houses. Site-finding history, kept because each failure taught the mechanism something real: (1) a first pick 80m out from a dead-end stub was 12m from a live railway -- construct.py had NO check for non-building infrastructure at all until this forced one (footprintClear/footprintConflicts on the report, now also checking waterways/water bodies after a second real miss below); (2) several picks further along that same heading were geometrically clear but sat on ground too steep for the router's state lattice to climb even one legal first step (router.py's documented 'wedge' limitation); (3) after adding real terrain benching (construct now builds a level pad -- convex hull of every part, benched UP to the max elevation sampled at its vertices, so the frontage ends up above the naturally lower ground beyond it rather than at unchanged grade), slope stopped being the constraint, and the next auto-picked clear site turned out to straddle a real stream -- construct's conflict-check didn't cover water yet, only found by looking at the render. Both gaps are now load-bearing checks, not just this op's history. Final site: clear of buildings, roads, rail AND water, benched to ~204m, with a short (34m) access road reaching a real junction.

REVERSED 2026-09-11: this decision was superseded. The plan changed from 'wipe the island for entirely new content' to hand-painting the island in Photoshop while keeping ~95% of the real buildings in place. The 2,341 feature rows this op removed from kurose.gpkg (798 buildings, 1,070 roads, 414 points, 59 landuse -- exactly what apply_demolish(op-0003) computes, including the 84-way road/rail graph cascade) were reinserted directly into the live store, id-for-id, under change_log batch_id restore-op-0003-20260911-165701. This op entry is kept for history, not deleted -- the decision it recorded was real and is why the sea-fort construct ops (op-0005, 0017, 0018, 0019, 0020/0026) exist at all -- but its EFFECT on the live store no longer holds. A future full replay of this log (e.g. tools/city-map/_apply_ops.py) would re-demolish the island and must not be run against kurose.gpkg without accounting for this.

ORIGINAL NOTE: Port Island removed entirely to make way for a sci-fi sea fort complex (siting is a later op, once offshore construction -- anchor-in-sea detection, land reclamation, causeway routing -- actually exists; see ideas/entries/offshore-construction.json). Unlike Kobe Airport, which had no single unifying feature and needed a land-content union, Port Island is already one coherent OSM place=island multipolygon relation (reclaimed=yes, wikidata Q1207766), so the demolish polygon is that relation's own real coastline geometry directly: buffer(50m) to catch piers/breakwaters right at the edge, then simplify(25m) -- same buffer/simplify numbers as op-0001, for a consistent coastline character. Verified against the real cached extract before writing: raw island area 8.378 km^2 (matches Port Island's real-world ~826ha), 2040 other features intersect the raw polygon (confirms real content, not a degenerate shape), 982m clear of the already-removed Kobe Airport island and 2068m clear of Rokko Island (op-0004) -- no risk of the 50m buffer bridging either gap. Applying it: 2028 features removed, 13 clipped, 84 ways pruned by the road+rail graph cascade (ops/demolish.py) -- every bridge connecting Port Island to the mainland is eaten back to its real junction, the same mechanism verified against Kobe Airport's dangling railway bridge. 0 features survive inside the polygon's 2m-shrunk interior.

Rokko Island removed entirely -- the second of the two islands cleared for sci-fi sea forts, alongside Port Island (op-0003); same methodology, same reasoning for why the two are independent, non-conflicting removals. Real place=island multipolygon relation (reclaimed=yes, wikidata Q579015), buffer(50m), simplify(25m). Raw island area 5.965 km^2 (matches Rokko Island's real-world ~580ha); 3052 other features intersect the raw polygon. 2068m clear of Port Island, so the two 50m buffers cannot interact. Applying it: 3045 features removed, 8 clipped, 19 ways pruned by the graph cascade -- among them the Rokko Liner elevated transit line and its viaducts (electrified, bridge=yes, exactly the class of feature op-0001's fix was written for), eaten back to real junctions on the mainland rather than left dangling over open water. 0 features survive inside the polygon's 2m-shrunk interior.

Pre-clearing the new compound's own footprint before construct runs. A real dry run of op-0026 first came back footprint_clear=False, footprint_conflicts=['highway=unclassified'] -- op-0016's own trace road (this session, part of the same map-editor submission) cuts across where the west wing sits. construct.py deliberately surfaces this rather than auto-clearing it (module docstring: roads/rail/water crossing a footprint are 'left for the operator to notice', unlike buildings, which ARE auto-demolished) -- this is that deliberate operator decision: clip whatever's inside the convex hull of the compound's actual buildings+apron (not the full fence outline, which would clear far more than the buildings themselves touch). A demolish-clip, not a full removal, so the rest of op-0016 outside this footprint survives untouched.
